# Regular Expressions

## Warm Up {.activity .smaller}

Fill in one letter per square. Each row, read left to right, must match its pattern, and each column, read top to bottom, must match its pattern. The whole string must match.

```{=html}
<style>
.reveal table.rx { table-layout:fixed; border-collapse:collapse; margin:20px auto 0; font-family:ui-monospace,Menlo,monospace; width:auto; }
.reveal table.rx tr, .reveal table.rx th { background:transparent !important; border:none !important; }
.reveal table.rx th { font-weight:bold; font-size:.8em; padding:4px 10px; color:#fff !important; }
.reveal table.rx th.col { vertical-align:bottom; text-align:center; white-space:nowrap; font-size:.7em; width:160px; }
.reveal table.rx th.row { text-align:right; padding-right:16px; vertical-align:middle; white-space:nowrap; }
.reveal table.rx td { width:160px; min-width:160px; max-width:160px; height:100px; padding:0; background:#fff !important; border:3px solid #29335c !important; }
</style>
<table class="rx" data-quarto-disable-processing="true">
  <tr><th></th><th class="col">(B|D)*A(B|D)*</th><th class="col">(A|R|O)*</th><th class="col">T(E|A)*(G|S)</th></tr>
  <tr><th class="row">(B|C)A(T|R)</th><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
  <tr><th class="row">A*R(E|I)</th><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
  <tr><th class="row">D(O|U)(G|E)</th><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
</table>
```

::: notes
BAT / ARE / DOG. Exactly one solution (checked by brute force in
planning/regex-game/crossword.py). No row can be solved alone: row 1 has 4
answers, row 2 has 2 (ARE, ARI), row 3 has 4.
A path: row 2 has length 3, so A*R(E|I) is A R ?, and the middle row starts with A.
Column 1: top is B or C, but (B|D)* allows only B. Bottom is D. So BAD.
Column 3: must start with T, so row 1 is BAT. (E|A)* rules out I, so row 2 is ARE.
Its last letter is G or S, and row 3 ends in G or E: G.
Column 2: A, R, then O or U; (A|R|O)* allows only O. So DOG.
:::

## Goals

* Read the regex shorthand: `+ ? {m} {m,n}`, classes `[...]`, `[^...]`, `\d`, `.`
* Get fast at reading a pattern: does it keep this string?


## Shorthand: How Many {.smaller}

Everything from here on is shorthand for something you can already write.

* `a+`: one or more. Same as \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
* `a?`: zero or one. Same as \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
* `a{3}`: exactly three. Same as \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
* `a{2,4}`: two to four. Same as \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

\

`colou?r` matches `color` and `colour`.

`ha+` matches `ha`, `haa`, … but not `h`.

::: notes
a+ = aa*. a? = a|ε: ε is the empty pattern, matching only the empty string.
Python writes ε as nothing at all: (a|) means "a or nothing", so colou?r is colo(u|)r.
a{3} = aaa. a{2,4} = aa|aaa|aaaa.
:::

## Shorthand: Which Character {.smaller}

* `[aeiou]`: one character from the list. Same as `(a|e|i|o|u)`.
* `[a-z]`, `[A-Z]`, `[0-9]`: one character from a range. `\d` means `[0-9]`.
* `.`: any one character.
* `[^aeiou]`: one character **not** in the list.

\ 

`[A-Z][a-z]*` matches `Tea` and `Latte`, but not `latte`, `LATTE`, or `Iced Latte` (the space!).

`c[^aeiou]t` matches `c9t` and `cxt`, but not `cat` or `ct`.

`...` matches any string of exactly three characters.

## Warm-Up: In or Out? {.activity}

`pattern = [A-Z]{2}\d{3}`

\

$L($`pattern`$)$ is the set of strings wholly described by the pattern.

Which of these strings are in $L($`pattern`$)$?

\ 

`CS110`

`ab123`

`DS2200`

`MA101`

\

::: notes
This pattern says: 2 capital letters, then 3 digits, and nothing else.
In: CS110, MA101. Out: ab123 (lower case), DS2200 (four digits).
Save DS2200: as a filter, contains keeps it, because DS220 is a part of it.
:::

## Standard Operators {.smaller}

Literals: `cat`

Dot: `.` any char (except newline)

Class: `[aeiou]` or ranges like `[A-Z0-9]`

Negated class: `[^,]` anything but comma

Alternation: `(cat|dog)`

Quantifiers: `a*` 0 or more, `a+` or more, `a?` 0 or 1, `{m,n}` range

Anchors (filters only): `^` start, `$` end

Escapes: a backslash makes a symbol literal: `\.` `\$` `\(` `\\`. But `\d` is a digit, not a `d`.

Groups: `(  )` captures, `(?:  )` non-capturing

Turn up the top card to start its pile. (A wild or a filter goes back in the deck; turn up another.)

## Pattern Eights: Play {.activity .smaller}

A pattern **keeps** a string when the _whole_ string fits it. `␣` on a card is a space.

On your turn, play one card:

* a **string** that the current pattern keeps, or
* a **pattern** that keeps the top string. It becomes the current pattern.
* a **wild**: write a pattern that keeps the top string. Not `.*`, and not the string itself.
* a **filter**, together with a string where _some part_ of the string fits the current pattern.
  The pattern stays.

Can't play? Draw one, and play it if you can. First to empty their hand wins.

**How?** 🤷 Anyone can ask, any time, for free. The player says what the pattern means in words:
"starts with a capital, and `Iced␣Latte` does."

**Check!** Still not convinced? Run it. A wrong play goes back to the hand, plus 2 cards.
A wrong challenge: the challenger draws 1.

## Check! {.smaller}

Settle a challenge here. Type spaces as real spaces.

```{pyodide}
import re

pattern = r"[A-Z]{4} \d{3}"
string  = "DSCI 220"

print(re.fullmatch(pattern, string) is not None)   # the whole string fits
print(re.search(pattern, string) is not None)      # some part fits: a filter card
```

# If there's time

## From Sets to Strings {.smaller}

Sets: $A=\{x\in U: P(x)\}$

\

A regular expression $r$ does two different jobs.

* **Language.** $L(r)=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches } r\}$.
  A set of _strings_, usually infinite.
  In Python: `re.fullmatch(r, w)`. In pandas: `df['col'].str.fullmatch(r)`.

* **Filter.** Keep the rows whose string has _some part_ that matches $r$.
  A set of _rows_, a subset of the dataframe.
  In pandas: `df['col'].str.contains(r)`.

\

Today: languages first, then filters.

## Regex vs. Language {.smaller}

Fix an alphabet of characters, $\Sigma$.

Then a pattern $r$ denotes the language $L(r)=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches } r\}$

* if no string matches the pattern,  $L=\varnothing$

* the empty pattern matches only the empty string ⇒ $L=\{\varepsilon\}$

* pattern `a` means $L=\{$`a`$\}$

* Concatenated patterns `AB` means $L(A)L(B)=\{xy:x\in L(A),y\in L(B)\}$

* Union of patterns: `A|B` means $L(A)\cup L(B)$

* Kleene Star: `A*` means all finite concatenations from $L(A)$ (incl. $\varepsilon$)

::: notes
Same spirit as set algebra: union / product / closure.
No anchors here: a language always means the whole string.
:::
